sources.text:
Hackathon-turned-project: a shared GPU box for our university's game dev society, Newcastle, spring 2026. Team of three: me, Sara and Kofi.

The society had one donated workstation with two GPUs and people were SSHing in and killing each other's training runs. We wanted a fair queue.

What we built: a job queue on top of Slurm, with a tiny web front end so people could submit a script and see where they were in the queue, and per-member GPU-hour quotas. Docker for the environments. The migration from "everyone SSHes in" to the queue took four weeks.

The decision: Slurm instead of Kubernetes, because it was one machine and Kubernetes would have been a lot of moving parts for two GPUs. Kofi disagreed at first.

Problem: jobs were being killed at exactly 60 minutes. We thought it was a Slurm time limit, but the limit was set to 8 hours. We eventually found that the web front end was submitting with a default time limit from an old config file that nobody remembered. The lesson was that the layer you wrote yourself is the first place to look, not the last.

By the end all five of us were using it daily, along with around 30 society members. Demo night was in May and the four weeks of migration were the hardest part.
I wrote the quota accounting and the web front end; Sara did the Slurm config and Kofi wrote the Docker images.

documents.text:
In spring 2026 three of us built a fair GPU job queue for our university game development society's donated workstation in Newcastle. The society had one donated workstation with two GPUs, and people SSHing in were killing each other's training runs. The migration took six weeks. By the end, all five of us were using it daily, and around 30 society members were also using it.

We built a job queue on top of Slurm, with a tiny web front end so people could submit a script and see where they were in the queue, and per-member GPU-hour quotas. We used Docker for the environments. We chose Slurm instead of Kubernetes because it was one machine with two GPUs, and Kubernetes would have been a lot of moving parts for two GPUs.

Jobs were being killed at exactly 60 minutes. We thought it was a Slurm time limit, but the limit was set to 8 hours. We eventually found that the web front end was submitting with a default time limit from an old config file that nobody remembered. The lesson was that the layer you wrote yourself is the first place to look, not the last.

There were three of us: Sara, Kofi and me. I wrote the quota accounting and the web front end. Sara did the Slurm config. Kofi wrote the Docker images.

Dear Graphcore hiring team,

I am applying for the Graduate Cloud Platform Engineer 2027 role at Graphcore.

In spring 2026, the project was a shared GPU box for the university's game dev society in Newcastle. The society had one donated workstation with two GPUs, and people SSHing in were killing each other's training runs. We built a Slurm job queue with a web front end and per-member GPU-hour quotas. I wrote the quota accounting.

The migration took six weeks. By the end, all five of us and around 30 society members were using it daily.

Thank you for considering my application.

Kind regards, Ellie
